reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker promotes joining Mirror Trading International through their team, claiming approximately 0.5% daily and 12% monthly returns and requiring Bitcoin participation starting at $100. The speaker also links a suggested $200 starting amount and recruiting one person on each side to binary qualification and additional payment. Daily-income graphics and a trading-result display accompany the promotion, though they do not verify the claimed returns or establish that funds were transferred or withdrawn.

citations.quote: AI trading bot (been out since Aug 2019) Avg. 12% monthly Fund with BTC Only
we've been averaging monthly 12%
You get paid in Bitcoin and trade for you when you make your money.
And once you get a person on your left and right at 100. You will be qualified for the binary and get paid that also

opening.argument: Judge the speaker's claims as investment commentary, not a promise that viewers will earn the same return. He qualifies the daily figure with "from what I've seen" and describes an average, while his account of the last day's result includes "I think." Those are descriptions of observed figures, not a guarantee of future performance. He also tells viewers to conduct their own due diligence. The claims deserve scrutiny, but this language leaves the decision with the viewer rather than presenting the returns as certain.

citations.quote: from what I've seen it's been an average daily of point 5
On the 29th, it was like 0. 53, I think.
you can do your due diligence and look at the videos on youtube

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited description states an average, not a guaranteed payout. Likewise, the speaker's account of Bitcoin payment and binary qualification describes what he says the program offers; neither quote establishes that anyone actually received those payments. His express invitation to do due diligence matters when assessing whether he presents the figures as beyond question.

citations.quote: Avg. 12% monthly
you can do your due diligence and look at the videos on youtube

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Hedging an estimate does not turn this into neutral commentary. The speaker says it costs $100 to start, recommends $200 for binary qualification, and tells viewers to join his team. Due diligence is mentioned, but it sits alongside a direct pitch for recurring returns and recruitment-based payment.

citations.quote: It's only a hundred dollars to, uh, start if you're going to start on my team. I suggest you start around at least 200 so you can get yourself. Binary qualified.
And once you get a person on your left and right at 100. You will be qualified for the binary and get paid that also
So if you're serious about Joining my team Let's get busy.

opening.argument: Much of the presentation walks through what the speaker says he can show in an account: he invites viewers into the trading pool, and a sampled frame shows a dated table with trading bonuses, closing balances and results. He also points interested viewers toward more videos and interviews. Read this as a demonstration of the interface and the speaker's reported experience. The visible entries show what the account displays; they do not by themselves establish that viewers will receive comparable returns.

citations.quote: Let's go into the trading pool, see what I can show you guys.
there's plenty of videos plenty of interviews plenty of everything for you to learn more about Mirror Trading International.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to a Bitcoin-funded offer and a recruiting condition, but those points do not exhaust what the video is doing. The speaker explicitly moves into showing the trading pool, and the account frame displays dated entries. The demonstration can be evaluated as a demonstration without treating its displayed results as proof of actual withdrawals.

citations.quote: Let's go into the trading pool, see what I can show you guys.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The account walkthrough serves the pitch rather than replacing it. The speaker says the displayed percentages prove people have been getting paid, then gives a starting amount, explains binary qualification and urges viewers to join his team. A table of reported results does not verify actual returns or withdrawals; it is presented in support of the solicitation.

citations.quote: show it proved that we've been getting paid around that margin
It's only a hundred dollars to, uh, start if you're going to start on my team.
And once you get a person on your left and right at 100. You will be qualified for the binary and get paid that also
So if you're serious about Joining my team Let's get busy.

opening.argument: The speaker describes a trading service with a separate team-based bonus: qualification requires a person on each side at $100. That structure can be read as a referral promotion attached to an offered service, not evidence on its own that deposits are diverted or that recruits are the source of every payment. A sampled frame shows an account page for adding funds, but an entry field does not establish that anyone deposited money or lost access to it. The record supports scrutiny of the offer, not a conclusion about an unseen transfer or loss.

citations.quote: And once you get a person on your left and right at 100. You will be qualified for the binary and get paid that also
You get paid in Bitcoin and trade for you when you make your money.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening identifies both the trading-return claim and the binary payment condition. It does not show where the advertised payments came from, or establish a completed deposit or withdrawal by a viewer. The funding page shows an amount field, not a completed transaction. Those limits matter when deciding whether the observed referral offer itself proves a fraudulent mechanism.

citations.quote: And once you get a person on your left and right at 100. You will be qualified for the binary and get paid that also

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Proof of a completed viewer deposit is not needed to identify what is being promoted. The description invites viewers to join a Bitcoin-funded trading bot with an advertised monthly average; the speaker recommends an initial amount for binary qualification and says recruits on both sides lead to additional payment. The funding page reinforces that deposits are part of the offered workflow. Calling the binary feature an ordinary referral bonus does not remove the recurring-return pitch.
